previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of gastroparesis following Nissen fundoplication was admitted for a two-day episode of nausea, vomiting, and increased bowel movements triggered by a fizzy drink. She presented with metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, and transient hypertension, all of which resolved with IV fluids, electrolyte repletion, and bowel rest. She was maintained NPO initially, treated with IV antiemetics, and enteral nutrition was restarted on hospital day 3. Her nausea improved, she tolerated a clear liquid diet, and was discharged home in stable condition. No infectious cause was found on stool or blood cultures. Discharge instructions included resuming home medications, advancing diet gradually, and follow-up with her primary care provider.

#Abdominal pain: patient presented with abdominal pain after an 
outside hospital upper GI series for second opinion regarding 
etiology/extent of gastroparesis with potential future plan for 
gastric pacer.  After this study patient developed profound 
nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain which was felt to be 
consistent with a gastroparesis flare due to large amount of 
barium.  Patient had a KUB which was negative for obstruction 
and revealed barium throughout the colon.  Patient had no 
diarrhea to suggest gastroenteritis.  Initial liver function 
tests were unremarkable except for an elevated alkaline 
phosphatase.  This should be repeated as an outpatient and if 
still elevated further work-up should be pursued including ggt.  
Patient's symptoms resolved with bowel rest and reglan/lorazepam 
for nausea.  On day of discharge she was tolerating a full 
liquid diet and was pain free.

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the hospital because you were having 
abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. This was consistent with a 
flare of your gastroparesis. This was likely due to the barium 
load you got with your upper GI series earlier this week. An 
x-ray of your abdomen showed the presence of barium in your 
bowels, but no obstruction. 

You improved with bowel rest. Liquid diet was restarted when you 
felt better. 

MEDICATION RECOMMENDATION:
Recommend taking Reglan over taking Zofran.  Reglan is a 
pro-motility type of anti-nausea medicine which may be helpful 
for gastroparesis.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, shortness of breath.  Please
evaluate for small-bowel obstruction.

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to abdominal x-ray performed ___.

FINDINGS:  Supine and upright abdominal radiographs demonstrate a normal bowel
gas pattern without dilated loops of bowel or air-fluid levels. No pneumatosis
or pneumoperitoneum evident.  Surgical clips present in the right and left
upper quadrants.  Residual oral contrast is noted throughout the colon and
within the rectum.  Partially imaged lungs appear unremarkable.  The aorta is
tortuous.  Heart size is normal.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of bowel obstruction.
